## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kinti Sutta* (MN 103; PTS MN ii 238) was delivered by the Buddha while residing at Kusināra [Dhammika, Middle Land]. It opens with the Buddha inquiring how his disciples perceive his motivations: he asks whether they imagine he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodgings, or different states of being [Gethin 2001; Dutt, Early History]. Reaffirming that his mission is guided solely by compassion and the spiritual uplift of his followers, he urges the Saṅgha to train united, in concord, and without dispute in the principles he has directly realized, specifically the "seven sets" of awakening factors (including the *satipaṭṭhāna*s and right exertions) [Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2003; Dutt, Early History; Watanabe 1983].
SuttaCentral lists no direct parallels for MN 103, and Anālayo confirms that no canonical parallels appear to be known [SuttaCentral; Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma]. However, related discussions on doctrinal harmony and settling disputes occur in the *Pāsādika Sutta* (DN 29) and the immediately following *Sāmagāma Sutta* (MN 104) [Gethin 2001; Tan 2004]. DharmaNexus records text reuse across 68 Pali works, most notably with the Vinaya Khandhakas (Kd 4 and Kd 14), DN 29, and several Aṅguttara Nikāya collections, alongside machine-generated cross-language alignments with the Tibetan *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* and Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26) [DharmaNexus].
